choices.A: Smoke, darkness, and salt

questions.explanation: The first paragraph names moisture, oxygen, and suitable temperature.
questions.stimulusText:
A seed may appear inactive, yet it contains a living embryo and a supply of stored food. Many seeds begin growing when moisture, oxygen, and a suitable temperature occur together. Others remain dormant even when these basic conditions seem favorable.
Dormancy can prevent a seed from sprouting at a dangerous time. Some desert plants produce seeds with coatings that water cannot easily enter. Months of weathering may weaken the coating, delaying growth until rainfall is more likely to continue. Certain forest seeds respond to a period of winter cold. This requirement helps keep them from sprouting during a brief warm spell in autumn.
Fire can also provide a signal. In several plant species, heat cracks a hard seed coat, while chemicals in smoke trigger changes inside the seed. Such adaptations allow new plants to emerge after flames have opened sunny space and returned nutrients to the soil.
Dormancy is therefore not simply a failure to grow. It is a timing strategy. By responding to particular environmental cues, seeds improve the chance that fragile seedlings will encounter conditions they can survive.

questions.stimulusText:
A first draft is often judged by what it lacks. Its opening may wander, its evidence may be thin, and its conclusion may arrive too quickly. Because the finished work looks smoother, the rough version can seem like an embarrassing stage best hidden from view.
Yet a draft performs a different job from a final piece. It makes thought visible. Once an idea exists on a page, a writer can test its order, notice gaps, and discover connections that silent planning did not reveal. Crossed-out sentences are not proof that writing failed; they record decisions.
This principle reaches beyond essays. An engineer's early model exposes weaknesses before expensive materials are used. A musician's rehearsal uncovers an awkward transition. In each case, the unfinished version creates a safe place for correction.
Improvement still requires discipline. Repeating the same attempt without reflection is not revision. The maker must compare the result with the goal and decide what to change. A draft has value not because imperfection is automatically admirable, but because visible imperfection gives purposeful work somewhere to begin.

questions.stimulusText:
Mara had practiced her cello solo for weeks, but the auditorium felt different when it was empty. Every scrape of a chair echoed, and the stage lights erased the audience seats beyond the first row. During the dress rehearsal, she rushed the opening and missed a shift she had played correctly at home.
Mr. Ibarra did not ask her to begin again. Instead, he walked to the back wall and asked Mara to play one sustained note toward him. She drew the bow slowly. The note traveled through the room and returned as a faint reflection. Then he moved to the balcony and asked for the same note.
By testing the hall, Mara began listening outward instead of only monitoring her fingers. She noticed that quick passages blurred when she hurried, while rests seemed shorter under the bright lights. On her next run, she allowed each phrase to reach the room before beginning the next.
The mistake in the opening did not disappear from her memory. It became useful information. When the audience arrived that evening, the hall was no longer an unfamiliar space waiting to expose her errors. It was part of the instrument she had learned to play.

questions.prompt: What information does an echo’s delay provide?

choices.A: the object’s exact color
choices.B: the distance to an object

questions.stimulusText:
Bats that hunt at night cannot always rely on vision. Many species use echolocation: they release high-frequency calls and interpret the returning echoes. An echo's delay indicates how far away an object is. Changes in loudness and pitch can provide clues about the object's size, texture, direction, and motion.
Producing a call is only the beginning. A bat must separate useful echoes from sounds made by wind, insects, other bats, and its own movements. Its ears and nervous system process these signals extremely quickly. As a bat approaches an insect, it often sends calls more rapidly, receiving updated information at shorter intervals.
Different surroundings favor different call patterns. In open air, longer calls can help detect distant targets. Near branches and leaves, shorter calls reduce overlap between outgoing sounds and returning echoes. Even bats of the same species may adjust their calls as conditions change.
Echolocation is sometimes described as seeing with sound, but the comparison is incomplete. It is an active process: the bat selects a call, receives a response, and changes its next call based on what it has learned.

As cities expanded, some small streams were straightened, covered, or directed into underground pipes. This created land for streets and buildings and moved storm water away quickly. Over time, however, buried channels sometimes became too narrow for heavier runoff, and residents lost access to natural waterways.
A process called daylighting brings a covered stream back to the surface. Engineers first study old maps, current drainage patterns, soil, and nearby structures. The restored channel may not follow its exact historical route because modern buildings and utilities occupy the land. Instead, designers seek a workable path that safely carries water.

questions.stimulusText:
Farmers and gardeners depend on plants that can thrive under particular conditions. Yet a crop variety may disappear when people stop growing it, when disease spreads, or when its habitat changes. Seed banks help preserve plant diversity by storing seeds from many varieties and wild relatives of crops.
Workers first clean and dry collected seeds. Lower moisture slows the chemical activity that causes seeds to age. The seeds are sealed in labeled containers and kept cold. Records identify where and when each sample was collected and describe important traits.
Storage does not keep every seed alive forever. Staff periodically remove a small sample and test whether the seeds still sprout. If too few germinate, workers grow some remaining seeds under controlled conditions, collect fresh seeds, and return the new generation to storage.
Seed banks are not replacements for farms or natural habitats. Plants continue to evolve only when they grow and reproduce in changing environments. Instead, stored collections provide a backup. Researchers may use them to study plant traits, and breeders may find useful characteristics, such as resistance to a disease. By protecting many kinds of seeds, banks preserve options that future communities may need.
